senses.explanation: **Very** goes before an adjective or an adverb and makes it stronger: *very big*, *very quickly*. It is not used before a verb (*I like it very much*, not *I very like it*) or before a comparative (*much better*, not *very better*), and it is not usually combined with adjectives that already mean the extreme, such as **huge** or **excellent**, which take **really** or **absolutely** instead. *Not very* before an adjective is a soft way of saying the opposite: *not very good* means bad.

examples.text: Thank you very much for your help.

examples.note: *not very*: a polite way of saying bad

synonyms.note: **really** is more informal and can also go before a verb

compare.note: **too** says more than is good or wanted; **very** only says a lot
in American English **quite** is close to **very**; in British English it usually means fairly, but completely before an adjective that already means the extreme (*quite amazing*, *quite perfect*)

senses.definition: used before the -est form of an adjective, such as **best** or **biggest**, or before **first**, **last**, or **next**, to make it stronger

examples.text: This is the very best coffee in town.
We met on the very first day of school.
This is the very last chance you'll get.
I'll see you on the very next corner.

phrases.definition: a lot; to a great degree
phrases.explanation: **Very much** comes after the verb and its object, or before a past participle: *very much appreciated*. It is the way to strengthen a verb, because **very** alone cannot go before a verb.

examples.text: I like the new apartment very much.
Thank you very much for coming.
Are you pleased with it? Very much so.

word_family.note: *the very end*, *at that very moment*: exactly the one named, and nothing else

usage_note: **Very** is also an adjective meaning exactly the one named (*at the very end*, *this very moment*, *the very idea!*, *my very own room*, *the very same street*), with its own entry: **[[very-adj|very]]** (adjective). Some writing guides treat **very** as the sign of a weak word: instead of *very big*, a stronger adjective such as **huge** may read better.

learner_errors.note: **Very** is not used before a comparative; use **much**, **a lot**, or **far**.
**Very** cannot go before a verb; use **really**, or put **very much** after the verb: *I like this song very much*.
**Unique** means one of a kind, so it cannot come in degrees; **really** or **truly** can be used for emphasis instead.

adaptation.semantic: **Very** is a pure degree word. Some languages use the same word for **very** and for **really** or **truly**; in English, **really** can replace **very**, but **very** cannot replace **really** before a verb: *I really like it*.
adaptation.grammar: **Very** goes before adjectives and adverbs, never before verbs or comparatives: *I like it very much*, *much better*. It is not usually combined with adjectives that already express an extreme (**huge**, **freezing**, **perfect**), which take **really** or **absolutely** instead.
adaptation.pronunciation: The first vowel is the short **e** of **bed**, and the **v** is made with the top teeth on the lower lip; it must not become **b** or **w**. The final **y** is a short *ee*.
